title: Correct the flame-temperature, exhaust-temperature and catalytic-converter claims in the automotive combustion path
question: PATH:SSF:CHE-AUTO-VERBRENNUNG-0001 (lib/learningPaths.ts; the same 2500 °C figure is repeated in PATH:SSF:PHY-AUTO-MOTOR-0001) teaches that gasoline (C8H18) burns at 'ca. 2500 °C', that exhaust gases leave the cylinder at 700–900 °C, and that a catalytic converter reduces pollutant concentration 'from 80% to below 1%'. What does the primary and technical literature actually establish for (a) gasoline composition and stoichiometry — is C8H18 a valid single surrogate for gasoline?; (b) the stoichiometric adiabatic flame temperature of gasoline/air and the difference between adiabatic, constant-volume peak, and measured burned-gas temperatures; (c) realistic exhaust temperatures at the exhaust valve/manifold, catalyst inlet and tailpipe under cold start, idle and load; (d) the lambda and temperature windows that produce CO, NOx and unburned hydrocarbons; and (e) three-way catalyst light-off, conversion efficiency, oxygen-storage and lambda-window behaviour, including what an '80% to below 1%' claim could legitimately refer to? Separate measured values, standard model calculations, and didactic simplification.
why_now: The path is a registered prototype and its quiz repairs test the same stoichiometry; the 2500 °C figure is repeated in PATH:SSF:PHY-AUTO-MOTOR-0001, so one correction affects at least two learner-facing paths and the NOXIA TOOL:COMBUSTION / SENSE:EXHAUST unlocks. The hard numbers are asserted without a source or uncertainty range.
real_world_anchor: Gasoline/air combustion thermochemistry and three-way catalytic converter performance: adiabatic flame temperature, exhaust gas temperature, lambda-dependent CO/NOx/HC formation, and catalyst light-off/conversion efficiency.
novelty_reason: No previous SSF research topic addresses combustion thermochemistry or exhaust aftertreatment. The closest topics are kitchen/caramel chemistry and critical-materials supply, which do not answer flame temperature, lambda-dependent pollutant formation, or catalyst conversion efficiency.
